Early Lessons in Strength and Fairness.
Before anyone ever knew the name Ruth Bader Ginsburg, there was just a quiet girl in Brooklyn, taking in the world from a small apartment filled with the smells of home-cooked meals and the gentle buzz of family conversations.
Picture a young Ruth, watching her mother move through each day with a kind of determined grace. Her mother had set aside her own dreams of education, but she poured all her hopes into Ruth—teaching her that independence and learning weren’t just nice to have, they were absolutely essential.
School quickly became Ruth’s second home. She’d sit up near the front, not to be the center of attention, but just to soak up every single word the teacher said. At night, she’d stay up late, pouring over her books, convinced that knowledge could open doors that most people never even saw. Her mother was her biggest supporter, always there with encouragement—but she was also firm about discipline and self-control. In a world that kept telling girls to stay quiet, Ruth learned to listen deeply, to choose her words carefully, and never to let anger get the best of her.
Then, loss came early. Just as Ruth was about to graduate from high school, her mother became seriously ill. The days at home grew heavy, and the apartment felt emptier with each passing week. The day before graduation, Ruth’s mother passed away. Instead of letting her grief swallow her, Ruth held onto those lessons—resilience, self-control, and fairness—turning them into a quiet strength that would shape her whole life.
When Ruth arrived at college, it felt like stepping into a brand-new world—one full of possibility, but also full of reminders that women were still expected to know their place. At Cornell, she found brilliant classmates, but she also noticed how the women were often expected to look for husbands rather than careers. Professors sometimes seemed to overlook her, calling on a male student even when her hand was up. But Ruth didn’t let that stop her. She found mentors who saw her potential, and she excelled.
And then she met Marty—a fellow student whose quick humor and warmth stood out right away. Their partnership wasn’t just about love; it was built on a real belief in each other’s abilities and dreams.
The world outside was changing, but it was slow. Ruth could see that the law could either keep old barriers in place—or help tear them down. She started to imagine a future where her mind and her efforts could make things a little bit fairer, not just for herself, but for everyone who’d ever been told to wait their turn.
Looking back, you can see how these early years—shaped by hardship, hope, and a mother’s unwavering belief—planted the seeds for everything Ruth Bader Ginsburg would go on to do.
